purpose: Define deduplicated logical candidates that have survived discovery and first source-level audit. This file is not the v1.8 production library and must not be read by scheduled reports.

items.source: Fodor, Patterson & Shank (2025), Anchoring bias in the NFL gambling market
items.canonicalClaim: Preseason expectations can remain associated with bettor behavior and sportsbook closing prices well into an NFL season; preseason anchors are therefore context, not independent current-value evidence.
items.strongestLimitation: Underlying data are not shareable and the study is game-market behavior rather than player-prop calibration.

items.source: Borghesi, Salaga, Williams & Mondello (2026), Contract choice, parlay adoption, and sportsbook margins
items.canonicalClaim: Parlay adoption rose sharply within bettors in a large regulated NFL wagering sample and higher parlay use was associated with higher sportsbook margins and bettor losses; multi-leg products require explicit margin/correlation caution.
items.strongestLimitation: One sportsbook operator; does not establish a universal same-game-parlay correlation-pricing rule.

items.source: Hegarty & Whelan (2025), Forecasting soccer matches with betting odds: A tale of two markets
items.canonicalClaim: Efficiency and favorite-longshot behavior depend materially on market structure: traditional 1X2 and Asian handicap prices for the same matches can have different calibration properties.
items.strongestLimitation: European soccer-specific evidence; do not transfer numerical effects to North American markets.

items.source: Clegg & Cartlidge (2025), Not feeling the buzz: Correction study of mispricing and inefficiency in online sportsbooks
items.canonicalClaim: A reported betting edge can be materially driven by a single erroneous odds observation and can fail out of period; data-quality correction and post-period replication are mandatory before treating a historical strategy as transportable.
items.strongestLimitation: The specific strategy is tennis-specific; the general lesson is methodological.

items.source: Montone (2021), Optimal pricing in the online betting market
items.canonicalClaim: Online bookmaker price changes can reflect demand elasticity and order-flow shocks as well as information; movement alone should not be interpreted as a pure informed-money signal.
items.strongestLimitation: Broad microstructure evidence rather than a sport-specific predictive rule.

items.source: Nofsinger & Shank (2023), Momentum trading in the NFL gambling market
items.canonicalClaim: NFL bettors exhibit aggregate momentum behavior, especially in totals, but observed momentum behavior does not imply a robust current predictive edge and reported trading outcomes are mixed.
items.strongestLimitation: Older 2003–2017 market regime.

items.source: Fodor, Onuk & Shank (2026), Do economically meaningful quote differences convey private information?
items.canonicalClaim: Crossing football key numbers 3 and 7 can create large demand discontinuities without corresponding return predictability; meaningful quote changes are not automatically private-information signals.
items.strongestLimitation: Contest contract data are not identical to sportsbook inventory and the result applies to football spread thresholds.

items.source: Baker, Balthrop, Johnson, Kotter & Pisciotta (2026), Retail Betting Markets
items.canonicalClaim: Modern retail betting markets are changing rapidly through technology, regulation and product design; historical priors require explicit market-regime transportability review.
items.strongestLimitation: Synthesis/context rather than independent predictive evidence.

items.source: Pitcan (2026), Does a Structural Model Add Anything to the Closing Price?
items.canonicalClaim: Model evaluation should test whether a forecast adds information beyond a de-vigged closing market, not merely whether it achieves respectable stand-alone accuracy.
items.strongestLimitation: Very recent preprint; requires replication before elevation.

items.source: Clegg, Song & Cartlidge (2026), A market-calibrated accelerated failure time model for in-play football forecasting
items.canonicalClaim: In-play forecasting should separate pregame market information from new in-play state information; market calibration can dominate raw structural-model improvements.
items.strongestLimitation: Only 140 EPL matches and a reported betting ROI that is not independently replicated; profitability claim remains quarantined.

items.source: Moshrefi (2026), Prices, Probabilities, and Parlays: Systematic Bias in Sports Prediction Markets
items.canonicalClaim: Probability calibration can depend on time-to-expiry and product type, and joint/parlay pricing should not be inferred mechanically from marginal leg prices.
items.strongestLimitation: Kalshi prediction-market structure is not sportsbook structure.

items.source: Wornow (2026), Betting on Performance
items.canonicalClaim: Direct FanDuel closing-prop evidence across multiple NBA stat categories does not support a simple universal over/under directional bias; player-prop History Fit should remain stat- and context-specific.
items.strongestLimitation: Undergraduate thesis, one sportsbook, and research design is not a full market-efficiency calibration study.

items.source: Papageorgiou, Sarlis & Tjortjis (2024), Evaluating the effectiveness of machine learning models for performance forecasting in basketball
items.canonicalClaim: Basketball player-stat forecastability differs by target statistic and model; points, rebounds and assists should not inherit one generic player-form error model.
items.strongestLimitation: Does not test sportsbook prices.

items.source: v1.8 targeted discovery and Phase 2 audit
items.canonicalClaim: No sufficiently strong direct scholarly WNBA closing player-prop calibration study has been verified; NBA direct-market confidence must not be inherited automatically.
items.strongestLimitation: Gap record; supports NR rather than a negative prediction.

items.source: Korkee (2025/2026), Using machine learning for player performance prediction in ice hockey games
items.canonicalClaim: Individual NHL shots on goal are sufficiently forecastable to justify a dedicated SOG mechanism layer using role and context, but forecastability does not establish sportsbook mispricing.
items.strongestLimitation: Master's thesis and no direct closing-price calibration.

items.source: Ding, Cribben, Ingolfsson & Tran (2021), Do NHL goalies get hot in the playoffs?
items.canonicalClaim: Recent goalie save-percentage hot streaks should not be treated as persistent save-probability evidence; save volume and save efficiency must be modeled separately.
items.strongestLimitation: Historical playoff sample and not a sportsbook saves-line study.

items.source: Deshpande & Evans (2019), Expected Hypothetical Completion Probability; Yurko, Nguyen & Pelechrinis (2024), NFL Ghosts
items.canonicalClaim: Receiving props should separate target opportunity, catch probability, defender context and yardage distribution rather than treating rolling receptions or receiving yards as stationary.
items.strongestLimitation: Tracking/forecast mechanism evidence, not direct sportsbook prop calibration.

items.source: v1.8 targeted discovery and Phase 2 audit
items.canonicalClaim: Strong NFL player-stat mechanism evidence exists, but robust multi-book closing calibration for regulated passing, rushing, receiving and anytime-TD props remains insufficient.
items.strongestLimitation: Gap record; supports NR or caveated mechanism fit.

items.source: Healey (2015), Modeling the Probability of a Strikeout for a Batter/Pitcher Matchup
items.canonicalClaim: Pitcher strikeout projections should incorporate batter/opponent strikeout tendency and matchup structure; pitcher K rate alone is insufficient, and game-level K props additionally depend on expected batters faced and workload/hook risk.
items.strongestLimitation: Per-plate-appearance event modeling rather than direct game-level sportsbook K calibration.

items.source: MLB Statcast Expected Statistics
items.canonicalClaim: Hit and total-base projections should regress recent results toward quality-of-contact information rather than rely on last-N hit rates alone.
items.strongestLimitation: Official performance metric, not sportsbook calibration evidence.

items.source: SmartStake MLB Player Prop Odds and Results (2026)
items.strongestLimitation: Direct dataset exists, but bookmaker/source classification, repeated unchanged quote minutes, game-key de-drift provenance, closing construction, grading, alt-line handling and calibration outputs must pass the reproducible audit before any market finding is admitted.

items.source: Walsh & Joshi (2024) plus 2025 corrigendum
items.canonicalClaim: Probability calibration remains a relevant evaluation concept, but original quantitative experiment claims must not be canonicalized until the published corrigendum and corrected code are reconciled.
items.strongestLimitation: Published implementation errors materially block unreconciled quantitative claims.
